analysis.one_liner: Requires hazardous waste facility owners to set aside real money for 30 years of post-closure cleanup.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote: it was referred to the House Commerce Committee in September 1996 and died in a subcommittee when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required companies that own hazardous waste treatment, storage, and disposal facilities to prove financial responsibility for accidents, corrective action, and at least 30 years of post-closure care after a site closes. It would also have barred companies from satisfying those requirements using financial ratio tests or a promise from a parent corporation, which can leave cleanup unpaid if the company's fortunes fall. It never left the House committee it was referred to.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near hazardous waste facilities and taxpayers generally: if a company cannot pay for decades of cleanup after closing a site, the burden of contamination falls on surrounding communities and on public cleanup programs. The bill would have made owners set aside real, verifiable money in advance.

how_it_helps.text: Requires a post-closure care period of at least 30 years wherever wastes or residuals remain on site, with the owner able to petition EPA to end it only after a public hearing demonstrating care is no longer needed [S2][S3].

Requires financial responsibility for credible accidents and known corrective action, plus liability assurances and funding for post-closure care, from the issuance of a permit through the entire post-closure period, with cost estimates revised when circumstances change [S2][S3].

For facilities closed after enactment, bars companies from meeting the standards through financial ratio tests or a corporate guarantee from a parent company — mechanisms that can evaporate when the corporation's finances do — instead of setting aside secure funds [S2][S3].
Says the bill's purpose is to 'improve public accountability and public safety in the management of hazardous waste facilities' [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Hazardous waste facility owners and operators, and their parent corporations, would bear the cost of securing real financial assurance — dedicated funds, insurance, or bonds — instead of relying on balance-sheet tests or corporate promises. Some of that cost could be passed through to customers of waste disposal services.
analysis.who_pays_short: Hazardous waste facility owners and parent companies

drawbacks.text: Requiring dedicated financial assurance for every year of a 30-year post-closure period raises operating costs for facility owners, and some of that cost would likely be passed to the companies and municipalities that pay for hazardous waste disposal; the bill text contains no cost estimates or transition aid [S3].

The bill eliminates parent-corporate guarantees and financial tests entirely for newly closed facilities, even though a well-capitalized parent can in principle be a dependable backstop; a good-faith objection is that the ban is overbroad and that EPA could tailor assurance requirements to risk rather than banning whole categories [S3].

The bill gives the EPA Administrator discretion to grant termination petitions after 30 years, which supporters of industry flexibility could argue invites prolonged, open-ended regulatory obligations for compliant operators [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core tradeoff is straightforward: secure cleanup funding costs companies real money now, while balance-sheet tests and parent guarantees shift the risk of unfunded contamination onto communities and taxpayers decades later. The bill addressed a real gap, though its flat ban on corporate guarantees for all newly closed facilities is a blunt instrument that raises costs even for financially strong operators.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Commerce Committee, which sent it to a subcommittee, and no further action ever came — it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Spratt Jr. (D-SC) introduced the bill on September 27, 1996, near the end of the 104th Congress [S1][S5].
It was referred to the House Committee on Commerce the same day, and no cosponsors ever signed on [S4][S5].
On October 4, 1996, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Commerce, Trade, and Hazardous Materials, where the action record ends [S5].
The 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997, with the bill still in subcommittee — no markup, no floor vote, no companion Senate action [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hazardous waste facility owners and their parent corporations, who avoided a requirement to post secure, dedicated cleanup funding for 30 years after site closure and could keep relying on financial tests and corporate guarantees.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Hazardous waste facility owners and parent corporations

for.name: Rep. John M. Spratt, Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on it

against.name: House Committee on Commerce
against.role: Committee of referral; never reported the bill out
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral, sent it to the Subcommittee on Commerce, Trade, and Hazardous Materials, and took no further action before the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill had zero cosponsors, so the record shows no measurable support or opposition from either party; it simply died in committee.

industries.industry: Hazardous waste treatment, storage, and disposal facility owners
industries.note: The bill would have forced them to fund 30 years of post-closure care with secure financial assurances rather than financial ratio tests or parent-company promises. Their interest in avoiding that cost runs against nearby communities, who bear the risk of unfunded contamination.

industries.industry: Parent corporations of waste facility operators
industries.note: The bill barred newly closed facilities from relying on a parent corporation's guarantee for closure, ending a mechanism that let subsidiaries operate without setting aside dedicated cleanup funds.

industries.industry: Surety and financial assurance providers (insurers and bond issuers)
industries.note: With financial tests and corporate guarantees ruled out, owners would have had to back obligations with instruments like insurance or bonds, creating demand for surety and fidelity products. Their interest runs alongside the public's interest in funds actually being there.
